notes.meaning: God spoke to Jeremiah during the fourth year of King Jehoiakim of Judah, around the time Babylon first invaded. The Lord gave this message so His warnings would be gathered together before the coming destruction.

God told Jeremiah to write down on a parchment roll every message He had given him over twenty-three years of ministry. Collecting these spoken sermons into a single book would give the people a clear summary of all God had warned.

God declared that hearing all these warnings together might lead the people of Judah to turn from their evil ways. If they repented, the Lord promised to forgive their sins and spare them from disaster. God always prefers to show mercy rather than bring judgment.

differ.view: God knows the future completely and without doubt, but uses words like 'perhaps' to show the proper purpose of preaching and to leave people without excuse.
God speaks in human terms here to show that His foreknowledge does not override human free will or force anyone's choice.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The conditional language reflects genuine human free will to accept or reject God's call to repent.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah summoned his assistant Baruch, an educated scribe, to write the scroll as he spoke the words. The Holy Spirit brought the prophecies back to the prophet's mind so Baruch could write them down accurately.

Jeremiah explained that he was held back from entering the temple courts himself. Whether he was barred by royal authorities or kept away by another obstacle, he was unable to deliver the message in person.

Jeremiah directed Baruch to go to the temple on a public fast day to read the scroll out loud. A day of fasting meant large crowds would travel from towns across Judah, giving the reading its widest hearing.

The prophet hoped that the solemn warnings would move the crowds to fall on their faces and pray for mercy. Turning from sin requires asking God for the grace to change before His severe judgment falls.
Baruch faithfully carried out every instruction Jeremiah gave him. He took the scroll into the temple and read the words of the Lord in the open courts.
In the winter of the following year, a special fast was called in Jerusalem because of a national crisis. People from all the surrounding towns came to the temple to plead for God's help.

Baruch stood at the upper entrance of the temple in the room belonging to Gemariah, a royal official friendly to Jeremiah. From this high room, he read the scroll aloud so the crowd gathered below could hear every word.
Gemariah's son Micaiah was present and listened carefully to the entire reading from the scroll. He recognized the gravity of God's message and immediately took steps to pass it on.

Micaiah walked down to the royal palace and entered the scribe's office where the chief government officials were gathered in council. These leaders included some from prominent families that had supported God's law in the past.
Micaiah reported to the council of princes everything he had heard Baruch read to the people in the temple. Sharing what affected him gave the royal advisers a chance to hear the warnings of God.
The royal officials sent an officer named Jehudi to summon Baruch with the scroll. Baruch did not shrink back in fear, but brought the document straight into their meeting.

The officials treated Baruch with courtesy, asking him to sit down and read the entire scroll to them. Baruch willingly read the warnings a second time so the rulers could examine the message for themselves.
As the princes listened to God's judgments, they looked at each other in deep fear. They realized the matter was too serious to keep secret, so they decided they had to tell King Jehoiakim.

Before approaching the king, the officials carefully questioned Baruch about how the scroll was created. They wanted to be sure these were Jeremiah's actual words from God rather than something Baruch wrote from memory.
Baruch answered plainly that Jeremiah spoke every word out loud to him, and he simply wrote it down with ink. This confirmed that the scroll was a direct recording of the prophet's inspired message.

Knowing the king's violent temper, the officials urged Baruch and Jeremiah to go into hiding immediately. They believed the message was dangerous to deliver, and they wanted to keep both men safe from the king's anger.

The officials placed the scroll in the scribe's office for safekeeping and went into the palace courtyard to speak with the king. They cautiously told him the substance of the prophecies before showing him the written roll.
King Jehoiakim sent Jehudi to bring the scroll from the scribe's room and read it aloud. The king and all his standing royal officials then listened to the prophet's warnings.

Because it was cold in the ninth month of the Jewish year, the king was sitting in his winter quarters beside a firepot of burning charcoal. Eastern palaces used these portable heaters to warm indoor rooms in winter.

Whenever a few columns of the scroll were read, the king used a scribe's knife to slice that section off and cast it into the fire. He kept doing this in defiance until the entire roll was reduced to ashes.

Unlike his godly father Josiah who tore his robes in sorrow when he heard God's law, Jehoiakim and his attendants felt no fear at all. They showed hardened hearts by refusing to show any sign of grief or repentance.
Three of the princes begged the king not to burn the holy scroll, but he ignored their pleas. Their brave appeal showed that some leaders still feared God, even though the king remained stubborn.
Jehoiakim ordered royal officers to arrest Jeremiah and Baruch so he could punish them. But the Lord protected both men by keeping them hidden beyond the reach of the king's search parties.
After the first scroll was destroyed, the Lord spoke to Jeremiah again. Human rebellion can never stop God from speaking His truth.
God commanded Jeremiah to take another scroll and write down every single word that had been on the original roll. Destroying the paper could not wipe out God's eternal word.

God addressed the real reason Jehoiakim burned the scroll: the king was furious because it predicted that Babylon would invade and lay waste the land. Rejecting a warning does not change the truth of what God has decided.

God pronounced a severe judgment on Jehoiakim, declaring that no son of his would establish a dynasty on David's throne and that his own corpse would be thrown out unburied in the elements. Jehoiachin briefly held the crown for only three months before being carried into exile, which counted as no real reign.

differ.view: Because no physical descendant of Jehoiakim could sit on David's throne, Jesus' physical descent came through David's son Nathan, while His legal right to the throne came through Joseph.

notes.meaning: God declared that He would bring the promised destruction upon Jehoiakim, his royal household, and all the people of Jerusalem. Because they refused to listen to repeated warnings, their stubbornness made their punishment certain.

Jeremiah gave a fresh scroll to Baruch, who again wrote down all the words from the prophet's dictation. In addition, God added many similar warnings to the new scroll, showing that fighting against God's word only increases one's judgment.
